Bungie unvaulting Destiny 2 content was a studio-saving emergency decision, because Marathon updates were never going to be enough
summary: At the last possible moment, Bungie takes a surprising and vital first step to winning back player trust.
body: Over the past couple of months, my Destiny 2 Fireteam has given me a tour of the Destiny 2 content I missed when I hopped off the train following the pandemic. When you play all the dungeons back-to-back, it's a buffet of delights—a concentrated dose of amazing and frequently obtuse FPS level design that you simply can't find anywhere else. A reminder that Bungie, pre-layoffs, was the very best at what it did. And yet, no game has had more caveats in its lifespan. There was always an amazing experience inside Destiny 2 somewhere , but recommending it to any normal person was out of the question. The onboarding for rookies was rough. Hoovering up all the expansions and dungeons was pricey and confusing. And after the release of The Final Shape, Bungie pissed off its player base repeatedly until the game was no longer sustainable. At what point would you ever advise a new player to jump in? Still, none of those issues compared to the content vault, first introduced in 2020. In removing entire campaigns from the game, not only did Bungie break players' ability to understand the complete story of Destiny 2, it also raised questions about the ethics of deleting content that you thought…

title: 'All roads lead back to Arma'
summary: Without Arma, gaming would look a lot different right now.
body: The ArmA family tree (Image credit: Future) This TikTok from Biffmatic (recently reshared by Bohemia Interactive) reminded me just how different PC gaming would look today if not for Arma, the long-running milsim series that's still going strong. Pretty much everyone knows that DayZ, one of the important PC games of the previous decade, began as an Arma 2 mod . The idea of PvPvE survival—the kind where you never know if you can trust the fella running down the road—was brand new, and it was such a hit that Arma developer Bohemia teamed up with DayZ creator Dean Hall to make a standalone version. DayZ went on to inspire a vibrant survival genre that's also given us Rust, Ark, and countless others. Did you also know that PUBG—and the entire battle royale genre, for that matter—is another Arma offspring? Brendan "PlayerUnknown" Greene developed the first version of PUBG as a mod to Dean Hall's DayZ mod. It was genuinely a mod of a mod, which Greene soon ported over to Arma 3. That mod was simply called "PlayerUnknown's Battle Royale" . It was my first introduction to the mode, and remains the mode I played most in Arma 3. Greene also consulted on H1Z1: King of the Kill before joining…

title: Rockstar asks modders to please take its games very seriously
summary: In mod guidelines published earlier this month, Rockstar tells modders to "respect our games."
body: What happened On September 10, Rockstar Games published new mod guidelines on its website, which it says are intended to "maintain a fun, creative, and welcoming place for players and content creators." The guidelines are seem primarily targeted at mods for the FiveM and RedM platforms, which Rockstar acquired —along with their developers—in 2023. Rockstar says mods must "respect our games": As part of its "right to set limits on how others can use our games and brand," the studio says mods can't expand or modify official storylines, missions, and characters, and can't combine settings and characters from different Rockstar franchises. Rockstar says modders can't incorporate other intellectual property or real-world likenesses, and forbids cheat menus or modifications that interfere with its official multiplayer and online services. Rockstar calls its official modding platforms "the exclusive licensed home for our community to monetize their mods," forbidding alternative monetization or commercialization of mods for its games. Do these guidelines have any teeth? Like Rockstar's more formal terms of service and platform license agreements , these guidelines are the sort of standard…

title: World of Warcraft: Forever players competing over enemies is 'extremely important' to the experience, Blizzard says: 'This is one of those things that we simply must hold the line on'
summary: Blizzard better have some clever solutions for launch day, then.
body: When the gates opened on the World of Warcraft: Forever beta, it was a free-for-all. Everyone fought to be the first to "tag" enemies with their attacks so they would count for their quests—a problem that is essentially obsolete in modern WoW. My memories of doing this in the real classic WoW came flooding back as I frantically tried to claim enemies before someone else did. But that old frustration also prompted old solutions: Whenever I came across a quest to kill seven wolves or whatever, I invited other players into my group so that everyone got credit. This, according to senior game designer Josh Greenfield on X , is exactly what Blizzard wants to see. Greenfield responded to a conversation about whether or not shared enemy kill credit should be a thing in WoW: Forever to say pretty firmly that it's not going to change. "This is one of those things that we simply must hold the line on," he wrote. "I think there are other things we can do to help alleviate some frustration here but shared tagging is not it." "It's hard to see the value in something like this when you are frustrated in the moment," he added, "but it is extremely important to our social pillar to maintain some o…

title: Bungie un-cancels Destiny: Vaulted content is coming back as new leadership promises 'Destiny is foundational to our future'
summary: "We are not done with Destiny."
body: Bungie's new leadership duo laid out the "next chapter of Bungie" today in a blog post with an accompanying video. The big news is that Bungie has essentially uncanceled Destiny 2, or will at least go the lengths to finally undo its greatest mistake: vaulting a bunch of raids and multiple of its story campaigns. Funnily enough, that work has already begun on the community side with a mod project that makes vaulted content playable through an offline build of Destiny. I got off the Destiny train a long time ago, but its "downward spiral," as PCG's Lincoln Carpenter put it in May , was a series of unforced errors that really began with the widely-hated decision to "sunset" (delete) gigantic chunks of the game in the name of "dealing with bloat." I still remember when a friend told me that the Destiny 2 campaign, I thing I bought and enjoyed in 2017, was simply gone. The news comes just three months after a brutal round of layoffs that affected hundreds of Bungie devs, essentially disbanding the Destiny 2 team. It's unclear if the studio will attempt to rehire the talent it shed with the shortsighted decision to call it quits on Destiny, but at least what's left of Bungie understands…

title: Touch grass? Not when AMD has whittled down ray tracing memory usage by 98% for these hardware-sapping bushes and trees
summary: I don't need to get out more.
body: As someone who spent a lot of their childhood talking to trees, I'm of the opinion that videogame forestry doesn't need to look any better than Alan Wake 2 's Pacific Northwest woodlands. That hasn't stopped AMD from innovating though; by leveraging 'tetrahedral cages' to help render a vast scene of greenery, researchers at the company say they've managed to cut the potential ray tracing memory usage by 98%. Typically, a scene of around 25,000 independently animated plants made of hundreds of thousands of triangles could hoover up 80 GB of GPU memory. Not only that, but it would take a Radeon RX 9070 XT GPU 300 ms per frame to check which surfaces within a scene are intersecting with a ray (the data structure that organises this information is called a Bounding Volume Hierarchy). In short, using traditional tech to render such a densely populated scene would be slow and choppy. Holger Gruen, a Fellow of AMD's Advanced Graphics Program, recently shared on GPUOpen that the team's tetrahedral cage demos only use "1.7 GB of BVH memory and approximately 3.3 ms for all BVH updates per frame" in comparison. Touch grass? Not when we've got trees like these. Anyway, let me break down how t…

title: I'm taking Insomniac's Wolverine patch as a sign: This is as bad as it's going to get
summary: A herald of the end, dressed in yellow.
body: I'm calling it here—this is as bad as it's gonna get. Insomniac's Wolverine has been getting slapped around a fair bit because it's perhaps the summit, the zenith—of 'how much handholding can you put in a game before we all get sick of it'. And listen, I've actually defended yellow paint on this site before. I am in agreement with most developers that a little guidance is good . Players do need environments that guide them, they do need the occasional bit of direction, and while they're smarter than Insomniac's given them credit for? They are also kind of dumb sometimes. But they aren't this dumb. I've seen clips of Wolverine that look ripped straight out of parody videos—Logan does not need a scent trail, red flashing lights, and a snow trail so cleanly placed it might as well have been left by Saint Nicholas himself. Game design trends like this tend to operate like a pendulum swing. It's happening in MMOs at the moment—the seasonal, frictionless structure is growing less popular than the desire for them to waste our time and test our patience again. Similarly, here. We're seeing the top of the arc before it all comes back to earth again. Insomniac walking back some of its handh…

title: Who the hell is buying their server memory from Amazon?! Also, can I interest you in a $101,000 kit?
summary: An X post just highlighted to me that Amazon really does sell everything.
body: This appeared on my X feed this morning and it's been bouncing around in my brain since I saw it. Titled as the "first $100,000 RAM kit" it caught my eye. The first thing to note is that this is, inevitably, server grade memory, and 2 TB of the stuff as well. It's DDR5-5600 of ECC RDIMM in a 16-pack kit for precisely $101,451.99 at Amazon , for all you server engineers out there. But the question that has been burning my bonce is who is buying their server farm memory directly from Amazon? But hey, Nemix RAM has been around a while now, and if it really is offering lifetime warranty on your $100k+ purchase that ain't bad. But surely, surely, you're getting a better deal from whoever you deal with, because if you're looking after datacenter hardware you must have been getting your kit from somewhere else originally, right? First $100,000 RAM kit 💀 https://t.co/oxI9q1fKd4 pic.twitter.com/9cKP39N7xz September 20, 2026 But then, I think we're probably at the point in the memory crisis where it really is any port in a storm, and people are getting memory wherever they can find it. So I guess this is just a sign of where we're at right now.

title: Kojima says his Sony split was amicable and they both still love us very much
summary: "We encourage you to take them with a dose of scepticism."
body: You do not, as a rule, see studios respond to rumours, reports, and speculation, but a recent Bloomberg report that Sony dropped Physint , Kojima Productions' upcoming stealth game, because it was overbudget and kept missing deadlines must have rankled the studio a little, because it released the statement above yesterday to quell fears. To quell fears of what? Well, mostly that the relationship between Hideo Kojima and Sony has gotten as bad as the relationship between Hideo Kojima and Konami, his erstwhile employer. Sure, says the studio, they might have split on Physint, but it was amicable. They'll probably even still spend Christmas together. Meanwhile, Xbox has swooped in for an easy PR win: picking up the cheque for Physint's continued development. All's well that ends well? summary: One must imagine a WoW player happy.
body: WoW Forever is basically my first time experiencing Blizzard's MMO for a significant amount of time—that level 13 Paladin rotting away on my retail account for the last eight years doesn't count—and you know what? Even as someone who isn't rocking around Azeroth in rose-tinted glasses, I'm having a pretty sweet time. I even surprised myself by how endeared I am to all its old-schoolness. I like that there's no globally shared tagging, even if that means you party with a handful of randoms for 10 seconds and never speak to them again. I've even been fine with its archaic gathering quests, where all of its nodes are server-side instead of client-side. Want to go and pick that cactus fruit, but some other player beats you to it? Well, it's gone now. Go and pick another one. Well, I was fine with it anyway. That is until I arrived in Orgrimmar, the Horde's capital city. My initial arrival was dizzying, bearing witness to its densely-populated streets and rapid-fire global chat where recruitment messages are quickly buried by folks talking about how many rolls of toilet paper they go through each day. title: Steam Frame's odd charging behaviour gets patched: cuts recharge times in half in some instances
summary: I choose to believe I had an infinitesimally minor role in making this happen.
body: A new version of SteamOS for Steam Frame has just landed. The company has fixed a few issues with the VR headset following its launch last week, which I'll get to in a bit, but one change stood out to me in the patch notes: Valve has added "substantially faster charging while unit is off / sleeping." I found the Steam Frame to be slow to charge during my time testing it ahead of my review. It took over two hours to go from totally depleted to fully charged (you can see the full timings in the battery section of my Steam Frame review ). When I installed a power meter between the charger and the outlet, it read just 11 W, which is much lower than the maximum output that could be delivered by the official power adapter, which is 45 W. So, I reached out to Valve with my findings. Mostly to see if this was some sort of protection measure for the battery's long-term health. Valve responded: "An empty battery takes around two hours to charge to full capacity. However, the charging is not linear. There is fast charging from 0 to 65%, and regular charging from 65% and up. Charging to 65% is expected to take less than 40 minutes. (Note: these values may be optimized over time, and are there…

body: Take a look at most modern PC gaming setups, and you'll find some RGB lighting somewhere. Did I miss something? There's no accounting for taste, as the old saying goes, so feel free to tell me in the comments what particular flavour of arr-gee-bee setup you're running. title: WoW devs surprised to find pure liquid nostalgia is popular
summary: "Betas for WoW aren't usually huge meter movers."
body: World of Warcraft: Forever 's beta has been utterly rammed with server issues —issues that I'm pleased to say were fixed in relatively short order, and one I certainly don't resent anybody for. What does jump my eyebrows up my head is the fact that its developers are shocked that the game's popular. For those not in the know, Forever's essentially Classic+. A version of the game as it was back in 2004, but with a bunch of changes made not to modernise it, but to make that old school vision better. Over 1,000 extra quests, new zones, redesigned talented trees, new racial abilities, and some major improvements to lighting. It's pure, distilled liquid nostalgia. A fat, juicy worm for shmucks (like me) to chomp onto and be shocked when there's a hook in our mouth—a fact that apparently completely disarmed the beta's development team: "AHMAGERD, this game is 20 years old, how do you still suck at this!?!" Rhetorically asks Tom Ellis, senior game producer, on X : "Heh, fair enough, short answer is, this is our BETA PTR environment stack, it's not a production stack by a long, long, long, long, long, long shot. Betas for WoW aren't usually huge meter movers so this environment just isn't…

body: When I first heard about this card-based roguelike city builder, I was confused. Then I played a round. And another. And another. And another. title: Solarpunk MMO Loftia is launching into early access November 3
summary: Live on your very own island in the sky.
body: How come the future in videogames is, more often than not, dark and gloomy? Where's the hope? Where's the optimism? It's all in Loftia, an MMO life sim with a delightfully cheery, eco-friendly aesthetic. And, as was just revealed at the PC Gaming Show Tokyo Direct, you'll be able to get your hands on it November 3. For those of you not in the know, Loftia is an eco-optimism life sim MMO that's been in development for the last four years. You and other players inhabiting the world will each get your own floating island to call home, and you've got a bunch of sustainable ways to decorate and power your slice of sanctuary. Wishlist Loftia on Steam Early access release date: November 3, 2026 Build a sustainable home on a sky island and work with your community to build the third space of your dreams. body: How cool would it be to wake up on an alien world with super powers? That's basically what happened to Superman himself. summary: I am being devoured by my own contradictions already.
body: Heads up, hotshot: you are being dispatched to a hostile alien planet. You will have to overcome life-or-death challenges that test your wits, physicality, and raw luck. You may die. summary: Please don't make me fight the trash pandas, I love them.
body: Never say I'm biased or I don't have an open mind, because here I am, telling you about a videogame where raccoons—my favourite animal on this Earth—are the enemy. Heartbreaking, I know. body: I can relate to the explorers in Core Keeper, because if I found an ancient, glowing orb, I know without a shadow of a doubt that I'd touch it, consequences be damned. summary: Clean freaks.

Early into the World Premiere trailer, showing the game off for the very first time during the PC Gaming Show Tokyo Direct, it seems very mundane at first glance as you clean your way around a Japanese apartment, little cash amounts floating off of each item as you scrub it and put it back in place. Then, it twists and music from Akira Yamaoka, composer of the Silent Hill games, kicks in and you see the dual nature of Dust till Dawn, which is not just a cleaning game but also a horror, somehow. title: Young Suns is an optimistic life sim for an unoptimistic time coming in November, and I'm already forming intense opinions about its cast of NPCs
summary: I would die for Nora. Sorry not sorry.
body: If you had to move to another planet in our solar system, which would you pick? Me, I'd go Neptune. I've always thought it's underrated, as our neighbours go, and it's a particularly pleasing shade of blue. I would die immediately due to cold and pressure, which I guess is a problem. I guess that problem is why the stars of Young Suns, which just revealed a November 3 release date at the PC Gaming Show Tokyo Direct, have elected to set themselves up on Jupiter. They're having a pretty cosy time of it, too: the game is a 1-4 player life sim about building a home for yourself in space, setting up a comforting nook for yourself in a vessel drifting over the face of the newly liberated gas giant. body: There is, you must admit, something a bit disconcerting about children's toys. summary: An expedition unlike any other.
body: The best art is all about descending into someone's twisted psyche. It doesn't matter who, but the deeper we get into their very being, the better. Now buckle up and prepare for Wane, a roguelike where you quite literally navigate through the deconstructed mind of Declan Wayne, a fading archaeologist.
